method: Flesch Kincaid grade plus five with a vowel-group syllable heuristic. Punctuated sentences and standalone task lines count as sentence units. Exact corpora and hashes retained. Headings, quantity-table fragments, staff text, dates, lesson codes and the verbatim scheme outcome are excluded. This guides editing and is not a learner assessment. Read-aloud and confirmed scribing routes are available.

Use actual Week 1 and Week 2 records. A photo supports appearance, not taste. Taste not tried and recorded means taste not assessed.
Add ingredient-use costs for the actual amount made. Divide a whole batch cost by its actual number of portions. An already per-portion price is not divided again.
Balance is built across the day or week. Each meal does not need exact plate sections. Use the actual dish and amounts in your review. These example portions do not meet every person’s needs. Choose water as a drink. No calorie counting, body or weight discussion is needed.
In your book. You may speak, sign, draw or direct an adult to record your confirmed words. Plan in any language.

Respond in your book or existing evidence record. Use your own words and the actual source. An adult can scribe and read your words back.
Name your actual dish or the true making stage. Give the dates and locations of your Week 1 plan and Week 2 notes or photo. Mark missing items.
Taste note present: use its exact meaning and source. Taste not tried and recorded: write taste not assessed. Describe appearance only if it is evidenced.
List actual amounts and ingredient-use prices. State whether the cost is already for one portion or for a batch. Show your calculation and check money left if using the £2.00 budget.
Name the food groups in your actual meal. Give one comment about variety or balance over time.
Name one real strength or limit. Suggest one future change, why it might help and how you would check it.
Give the date, evidence page or record location and actual support. Read or hear the review back and correct it if needed.
No food or tasting is needed today. Missing evidence stays pending. A model is practice, not your actual result.

Use the source before making a claim. These are adult examples, not pupil findings.
A The photo shows a folded wrap. B The recorded note says mild flavour. C There is no taste note.
Decide appearance, taste, or taste not assessed. Keep each claim with its source.
No food is needed today. Do not bring or taste the Week 2 food a week later. Use the actual Week 2 notes or a checked food-only photo. If taste was not tried and recorded, write taste not assessed. A photo cannot prove taste. Any fresh tasting would be a separate, newly cleared food activity and is not required here.

Week 1 model prices are invented for the stated amounts used by one person. They are not whole-pack shopping prices. The 60 g yoghurt is counted once, split as about 20 g in the filling and 40 g alongside. Use the pupil’s actual approved ingredient amounts and substitutions. Unknown costs stay unknown.
From a £2.00 budget, the one-portion model leaves 60p.
A two-portion batch at 280p costs 280p divided by 2 = 140p per portion. Do not divide a one-portion price again.
Replacing the 30p apple with a 35p pear gives 140p - 30p + 35p = 145p or £1.45. This leaves 55p.
In your book, use your actual listed amounts, known ingredient-use prices and actual portion count. Mark an unknown amount or price clearly.

Use this adult model to help review your actual dish.
Balance is built across the day or week. Each meal does not need exact plate sections. Use the actual dish and amounts in your review. These example portions do not meet every person’s needs. Choose water as a drink. No calorie counting, body or weight discussion is needed.
Name the food groups present in your actual ingredients. Explain one strength or a useful change in variety. Check a proposed substitution before future food use. Do not claim that a picture proves amounts or individual nutritional needs.

Use an actual finding or a named limit in your evidence. Choose one change that can be checked next time.
My evidence says or shows ___. I would change ___. This might help because ___. Next time I would check ___.
I have the ingredient plan but no recorded taste note. Taste is not assessed. Next time I would record an optional taste comment on the making day, or record that tasting was declined. This would keep the next review accurate. No tasting is required.
The pear version costs £1.45 rather than £1.40. It still fits the £2.00 budget. If fruit choice was the aim, I would choose the version that fits the person’s checked needs and preference. The extra 5p is a cost trade-off, not proof of better taste.
Give your own improvement and reason. Keep an expected effect separate from a tested result. A future food change needs an adult check before use.

Use these prompts in your book with your actual evidence. No food is needed.
Find the actual plan, cost record, safe-working notes and any checked food-only photo. Name what is present and what is missing.
Use a recorded taste note only for taste. Use a photo or actual plate record for appearance. Recheck the portion cost and food groups.
Name a real strength or limit, then one useful change and why. Say how you would check whether the change helped.
Choose one strength or limit. Give one future improvement, a reason and a way to check it. A prediction is not a result.
No food is needed today. Do not bring or taste the Week 2 food a week later. Use the actual Week 2 notes or a checked food-only photo. If taste was not tried and recorded, write taste not assessed. A photo cannot prove taste. Any fresh tasting would be a separate, newly cleared food activity and is not required here.
